section_title: What did Moses do when the promised rescue seemed farther away?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 15 So the Israelite foremen went and appealed to Pharaoh: “Why are you treating your servants this way? 16 No straw has been given to your servants, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” 17 “You are slackers!” Pharaoh replied. “Slackers! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’ 18 Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” 19 The Israelite foremen realized they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.”

20 When they left Pharaoh, they confronted Moses and Aaron, who stood waiting to meet them. 21 “May the LORD look upon you and judge you,” the foremen said, “for you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!”

22 So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me? 23 Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not delivered Your people in any way.”

context_lines: The Israelite foremen appeal to Pharaoh. They explain that they are being beaten for failing to make bricks while being denied the straw needed for the work. Pharaoh repeats his accusation of laziness and refuses to change the quota.

On leaving, the foremen confront Moses and Aaron. They ask the LORD to judge the brothers for making them offensive to Pharaoh and putting their lives in danger. The people who had bowed in worship at the end of chapter 4 are now represented by leaders who blame the messengers for their suffering.

Moses turns back to the LORD with his own anguished questions. Why has God brought trouble upon the people, and why did He send Moses? Since Moses spoke in His name, Pharaoh has done them harm and no deliverance has come. The chapter ends with that unresolved complaint; God’s answer begins in chapter 6.
common_interpretation_lines: The teachers agree that Moses is struggling with the gap between God’s promise and the suffering he sees, but assess his response differently. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) emphasizes his difficulty reconciling events with the promise and urges people in such distress to turn to God in prayer. [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/exodus/5.htm) gives a stronger reading: he understands Moses as returning in bitterness and wanting to abandon the commission. These are different assessments of the complaint, whose questions the passage records directly.
god_plan_lines: Scripture gives other examples of people crying out while they wait for God’s help. [Psalm 13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/13.htm) moves from repeated questions about how long God will seem absent to trust in His faithful love. It gives words to suffering that has not yet been resolved.

[Romans 8:18–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/8.htm) places waiting within God’s larger purpose for His children and creation. Believers groan as they wait for the redemption of their bodies, while creation awaits freedom from decay. The Exodus tells of a promised rescue that is still unfolding; Romans looks ahead to a fuller freedom, when suffering and decay themselves are overcome.
